title: ABG case 01
حالة غازات دم 01
vignette: A patient with a severe asthma exacerbation, working hard to breathe, now tiring.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: The low pH and raised PaCO2 indicate respiratory acidosis. At PaCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- of 26 mEq/L fits the small rise expected in an acute disturbance. In this patient with severe asthma and increasing fatigue, the rise in PaCO2 is a warning sign that requires urgent escalation.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 65 mmHg on FiO2 0.4 gives a P/F ratio of 162.5.
evidenceSources: Merck Manual Professional Edition. Acid-Base Disorders, expected compensation table and diagnosis. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nephrology/acid-base-regulation-and-disorders/acid-base-disorders
BTS/SIGN. Management of acute asthma in adults (2019), severity criteria. https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/document-library/guidelines/asthma/btssign-asthma-guideline-quick-reference-guide-2019/

title: ABG case 02
حالة غازات دم 02
vignette: A patient with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
options: Metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
question.explanation: Low HCO3- accounts for the acidemia. Winter's formula (1.5 × 9 + 8 ± 2) predicts PaCO2 of 19.5–23.5 mmHg. The observed PaCO2 of 22 mmHg is within that range.

evidenceSources: Merck Manual Professional Edition. Acid-Base Disorders, expected compensation table and diagnosis. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nephrology/acid-base-regulation-and-disorders/acid-base-disorders
ADA, EASD, JBDS, AACE and DTS. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (2024). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11272983/

title: ABG case 03
حالة غازات دم 03
vignette: An anxious patient hyperventilating after a panic episode.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: Low PaCO2 explains the alkalemia. HCO3- of 22 mEq/L is compatible with the small fall expected in acute respiratory alkalosis. The history helps explain the pattern. Assess the patient and consider other causes of hyperventilation before attributing it to anxiety.

evidenceSources: Merck Manual Professional Edition. Acid-Base Disorders, expected compensation table and diagnosis. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nephrology/acid-base-regulation-and-disorders/acid-base-disorders

title: ABG case 04
حالة غازات دم 04
vignette: A patient with prolonged vomiting and nasogastric suction losses.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
options: Metabolic alkalosis with expected respiratory compensation
No evident acid–base disturbance on this panel
question.explanation: Elevated HCO3- accounts for the alkalemia. For a rise in HCO3- from 24 to 34 mEq/L, the expected PaCO2 is approximately 46–47.5 mmHg. The observed PaCO2 of 46 mmHg fits that response. Vomiting and gastric suction provide a plausible mechanism.

evidenceSources: Merck Manual Professional Edition. Acid-Base Disorders, expected compensation table and diagnosis. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nephrology/acid-base-regulation-and-disorders/acid-base-disorders

title: ABG case 05
حالة غازات دم 05
vignette: A patient with longstanding COPD, at their usual baseline, feeling well.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
options: Metabolic alkalosis with expected respiratory compensation
Chronic respiratory acidosis with expected renal compensation
question.explanation: PaCO2 is 60 mmHg. In chronic respiratory acidosis, a 20 mmHg rise above 40 is expected to raise HCO3- by about 6–8 mEq/L from a baseline of 24. The observed HCO3- of 31 mEq/L fits, and the history supports chronicity. The mildly low pH is compatible with chronic respiratory acidosis despite the expected rise in bicarbonate.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 58 mmHg on FiO2 0.28 gives a P/F ratio of 207.1.
evidenceSources: Merck Manual Professional Edition. Acid-Base Disorders, expected compensation table and diagnosis. https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nephrology/acid-base-regulation-and-disorders/acid-base-disorders

vignette: A patient in septic shock with lactic acidosis, now also showing early respiratory fatigue.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
options: Metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
question.explanation: HCO3- of 12 mEq/L indicates metabolic acidosis. Winter's formula predicts PaCO2 of 24–28 mmHg. The observed PaCO2 of 48 mmHg indicates a concurrent respiratory acidosis. This combination and the patient's respiratory fatigue require urgent escalation.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 70 mmHg on FiO2 0.5 gives a P/F ratio of 140.
